limitations: Data collection in some classrooms involved conducting measurements more than two times, with some variations in student groups across these sessions. On the other hand, some classrooms were only measured once due to the limited availability of lecture slots appropriate for the survey.
Further research is required to study the combined effect of thermal and acoustic comfort on the overall indoor environmental quality of naturally ventilated classrooms.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical field study investigated the impact of acoustic environment and students' noise sensitivity on acoustic comfort, productivity, and engagement in 11 naturally ventilated university classrooms in a warm-humid climate. Key findings indicate that background noise (BGN), reverberation time (RT), and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) significantly influence acoustic comfort, with students reporting discomfort at BGN levels exceeding 62.4 dBA, RT above 1.7 s, and SNR below 3.7 dBA, especially those with high noise sensitivity. Conversely, students were more likely to accept conditions with BGN ≤ 61 dBA, RT < 0.7 s, and SNR ≥ 6.5 dBA. Acoustic comfort positively correlated with engagement and productivity. The study acknowledges limitations such as varying student groups across sessions and the need for further research into the combined effects of thermal and acoustic comfort.
